lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the US-China tech war
lead.head: Chips off the old bloc

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 64

play.label: Hear the war in six moves

body: Ajay Shah’s most amaz­ing pur­chase of the years be­fore 1991 was an early chess com­puter. You moved the pieces, an LED blinked, and it told you its move. A neigh­bour fly­ing to Singapore had brought it back. Amit Varma had the same one.

You would think such hunt­ing was a dis­tant mem­ory, Shah said. Instead it is back, in Shanghai and in Kazakhstan, and this time the prize is chips. “You are now back to a black mar­ket for mi­crochips,” he said. {064-S01}
The cul­prit this time is not Indian pro­tec­tion­ism but American ex­port con­trols aimed at China, the sub­ject of the episode: what the hosts call the global tech wars.
## From friends to foes

Until about 2016, Varma said, Democrats and Republicans agreed that free trade was good and that America should en­gage with China. Doubts began in­side the Obama ad­min­is­tra­tion. Donald Trump won with sim­ple nar­ra­tives that were wrong but easy to grasp. Joe Biden promised to re­verse him, then sided with his hawks.
“In just eight years, ev­ery­thing is switched around,” Varma said, “and the con­sen­sus now is that we are at war with China.” {064-C01}
The war, he said, stands on a three-legged stool: in­dus­trial pol­icy, tar­iffs and ex­port con­trols.

The con­trols are the sharpest leg. Shah said the only com­pa­ra­ble prece­dent is the West’s block­ade of the USSR be­fore 1989. Today any com­pany any­where that uses American tools to do work for a Chinese cus­tomer can be sanc­tioned.
## Why it went to hell

Shah traced the turn to mis­be­haviour mul­ti­plied by size. China, he said, by and large cheated on its WTO prom­ises, and stole in­tel­lec­tual prop­erty. India mis­be­haved on trade too, but India was small. China be­came sys­tem­i­cally im­por­tant.
Then Russia in­vaded Ukraine, with weapons built in fac­to­ries that held German ma­chine tools and Western elec­tron­ics, and Xi Jinping backed the in­va­sion while rat­tling sabres over Taiwan.
Shah is sym­pa­thetic to the re­sponse. “It is bet­ter to do eco­nomic war­fare than to do real war­fare,” he said. {064-C07}

Varma is not. A se­lec­tive glob­al­i­sa­tion, he ar­gued, is no more glob­al­i­sa­tion than crony cap­i­tal­ism is cap­i­tal­ism, and eco­nomic war­fare hurts or­di­nary peo­ple on both sides. “To me eco­nomic war­fare is eco­nomic war­fare,” he said, “and I’m fun­da­men­tally against eco­nomic war­fare at all times.” {064-C08}
## What comes next

Export con­trols helped the West win the Cold War, Shah said, but a de­ter­mined coun­try can string many cheap chips to­gether in par­al­lel. Against a fixed tar­get such as a nu­clear bomb, the bans only add delay and pain.

Where they can bite is in races: the drone war over Ukraine, ar­tillery, win­ner-takes-all mar­kets. “You don’t need to in­def­i­nitely be bet­ter,” Shah said. “You only need to be a lit­tle bit bet­ter.” {064-C12}
Whether it will work against China, he stressed, the jury is still out.

Varma warned of re­flex­iv­ity. Squeezing China could make it more des­per­ate over Taiwan, and its push into legacy chips could sink ri­vals, India’s chip am­bi­tions in­cluded. “All of this ra­tio­nale sounds great,” he said, “but un­in­tended con­se­quences will com­pound.”
Shah agreed that there would be sur­prises. When the hosts re­con­vene on the sub­ject in a year, he said, “we’ll get caught by sur­prise”.

Their read­ing lists ended the episode on China it­self. Varma rec­om­mended two books by Yuen Yuen Ang, re­ject­ing a “good ver­sus evil” view of a deeply com­plex coun­try. Shah chose an in­ter­view with Michael Pettis, call­ing it “ab­so­lutely eye open­ing”.

second.label: America and China
second.head: A mission, not a deal
second.deck: Ajay Shah says US engagement with China was idealism, not just realpolitik

pic.caption: President and Mrs. Nixon visit the Great Wall of China in 1972

body: American en­gage­ment with China was never only about in­ter­ests and re­alpoli­tik, Ajay Shah said. It was ide­al­ism, of a kind Indians find hard to pic­ture, and he has seen it face to face. {064-C04}

After Richard Nixon re-established eco­nomic re­la­tions in 1972 and Deng Xiaoping came to power in 1978, American so­ci­ety and the state signed on to “the China project”. After the USSR col­lapsed in 1989, the mood was that 2,000 years of fight­ing be­tween Persia and Athens had ended, and Athens had won. {064-J06}

China, the think­ing went, would wise up into a free-market lib­eral democ­racy, given time. So the West gave it ac­cess to sci­ence, tech­nol­ogy and trade, and Bill Clinton cham­pi­oned its entry into the WTO.

quote.text: All through the twen­ti­eth cen­tury there has been a sense in America that China is our re­spon­si­bil­ity

third.head: Deng gets a split verdict

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Deng Xiaoping’s record

body: Ajay Shah says Deng Xiaoping failed. His dream of turn­ing China into a nor­mal coun­try, Shah ar­gued, fell apart when Xi Jinping con­cen­trated power and China went back to being a com­mu­nist coun­try. {#dengfailed}
Amit Varma strongly dis­agrees. Deng, he said, is one of the great men of his­tory. “Hundreds of mil­lions of peo­ple out of poverty means hun­dreds and mil­lions of suc­cesses.” {064-C09}

Deng also made a bet­ter po­lit­i­cal out­come more likely than a Mao-like fig­ure would have, Varma ar­gued. Blaming him for Xi, he said, is like say­ing Nehru failed had Indira Gandhi not called off the Emergency.

Shah held his ground: if Donald Trump won and can­celled democ­racy, he would say the US Constitution had not de­liv­ered the goods. “I can’t dis­agree more strongly,” Varma replied, “but we’ll move on.” {#disagree}

box.title: The man who doubled down
box.text: As the China model was col­laps­ing, Ajay Shah said, Xi Jinping chose to side with Russia, keep rat­tling sabres over Taiwan and in­sist on the right to in­vade. He gave the West no re­as­sur­ance that China was not a rogue na­tion. {#xi}

sections.label: The great drama
sections.head: Eight years, one about-turn
sections.caption: the bipartisan U-turn on China
body: Until re­cently, Amit Varma said, there was a bi­par­ti­san con­sen­sus in the US: free trade is a good thing, and America should en­gage with China. It was al­most like the end of his­tory, to use Francis Fukuyama’s “often mis­in­ter­preted phrase”. {064-J05}

Around 2016, even be­fore the elec­tion, voices in­side the Obama ad­min­is­tra­tion began to ques­tion it, in­clud­ing Jake Sullivan, now the na­tional se­cu­rity ad­viser. “So it wasn’t as if ev­ery­thing hap­pened with Trump,” Varma said.

Donald Trump, he ar­gued, rose on sim­ple nar­ra­tives that were wrong but that peo­ple could get, es­pe­cially in a Midwest that had lost jobs: im­mi­grants are tak­ing your job, and your jobs are being shipped over­seas.
## Where you sit

Joe Biden said in 2019 that he would re­verse Trump’s poli­cies. In of­fice, his team split. Janet Yellen, his trea­sury sec­re­tary, wanted to en­gage China and lower tar­iffs. Katherine Tai, his trade chief, wanted them higher, and “per­haps where you stand de­pends on where you sit”, Varma said. {064-J08}
In the end, Varma said, Biden agreed with Sullivan, and America went in that di­rec­tion. Now, for the first time, the bi­par­ti­san con­sen­sus points the op­po­site way. {064-C01}
~ Varma drew on a piece by Greg Ip in the *Wall Street Journal*, and said the first draft of this his­tory is being writ­ten right now.

sections.label: How it is fought
sections.head: Three legs to stand on
sections.caption: the reach of export controls
body: America’s cam­paign, Amit Varma said, is a three-legged stool. First comes in­dus­trial pol­icy with heavy sub­si­dies: TSMC of Taiwan an­nounced in 2020 a fab in Arizona, and with sub­si­dies is now open­ing three. {#tsmc}

India tried in­dus­trial pol­icy in the fifties and six­ties, Varma noted, “and it’s not a good way to think about the world”. The sec­ond leg is tar­iffs, which rose under both Trump and Biden. The third is ex­port con­trols, to stop the flow of chips and in­tel­lec­tual prop­erty. Chips mat­ter be­cause so much sci­ence now hap­pens by sim­u­la­tion at scale. {064-C02}
## The long arm

Ajay Shah said the only real anal­ogy is the West’s pre-1989 block­ade of the USSR; Japan, Holland and Germany now sing the same tune. ASML’s most ad­vanced chip­mak­ing ma­chines can­not go to China or Russia. Nor can American de­sign soft­ware, and all the world’s semi­con­duc­tor work, he said, runs on three American soft­ware sys­tems. {#software}
An Indian firm using those tools to de­sign chips for a Chinese cus­tomer would be sanc­tioned too. {064-C03} American cit­i­zens and green-card hold­ers may not work in these sec­tors in China.

~ Varma sin­gled out the Foreign Direct Product Rule as par­tic­u­larly per­ni­cious. Under it, goods made abroad with American tech­nol­ogy or soft­ware count as American, even if they never cross the bor­der. {#fdpr} Its first tar­get was Huawei.

quote.text: It is an amaz­ing depth of ex­port con­trols that is sought to be im­posed upon not just China, but the whole world.

sections.label: The why
sections.head: Too big to misbehave
sections.caption: why the West turned on China
body: Ajay Shah began with ide­al­ism. America felt it had a civil­is­ing mis­sion in China, he said, and hoped it would be­come a lib­eral democ­racy. Under Xi Jinping, he said, that project fell apart. Shah says Deng Xiaoping failed; Amit Varma, who calls Deng one of the great men of his­tory, strongly dis­agrees.
Then bad be­hav­iour piled up. By and large, China cheated on the prom­ises it made on join­ing the WTO. There was gov­ern­ment-backed theft of soft­ware, and cyber at­tacks by China and Russia.

India, Shah said, has been a prime ex­po­nent of mis­be­haviour on trade too, de­mand­ing open­ness while stay­ing pro­tec­tion­ist. But it did not mat­ter: “India is in­con­se­quen­tial.” China be­came sys­tem­i­cally im­por­tant. {064-C05}
## The war that changed minds
Then Russia in­vaded Ukraine, a war that, Shah said, could cred­i­bly be called funded by European gas pur­chases. Why, peo­ple asked, fight a threat the West had it­self en­abled?

Xi Jinping dou­bled down, back­ing Russia and re­serv­ing the right to in­vade Taiwan. China came to be seen as a re­vi­sion­ist power: one, Shah ex­plained, that ques­tions the in­ter­na­tional order and seeks to dis­rupt it by force. {#revisionist}
~ Shah sep­a­rated three sto­ries that often get mixed up: the third glob­al­i­sa­tion, the tech war that began in 2022, and a short-term Chinese prob­lem of over­pro­duc­tion. {064-C14}

quote.text: China be­came big. China be­came sys­tem­i­cally im­por­tant.

sections.label: The quarrel
sections.head: Better than bullets?
sections.caption: economic warfare
body: Ajay Shah is sym­pa­thetic to the West’s rea­son­ing. As an econ­o­mist he wants world peace and full glob­al­i­sa­tion, he said, but if the choice is be­tween killing peo­ple and in­ter­fer­ing with a rogue power’s pros­per­ity, he will take the sec­ond. {064-C07}
With a hot war under way, and Xi Jinping never back­ing away from his claim on Taiwan, he called the tech war a rea­son­able strat­egy.

Amit Varma is not con­vinced. Freedom and vol­un­tary ex­change, he ar­gued, should be foun­da­tional, not con­tin­gent. And who sets the rules America claims to en­force? “Who de­fines a frickin’ global order?” he asked. {#frickin}
Trade is pos­i­tive-sum, Varma said. When the Swiss keep zero tar­iffs on Indian goods while India keeps its own, it is no favour to India: “They’re doing it for their own ben­e­fit.”
## Doctors and drones

One an­swer to China’s drone dom­i­nance, Varma said, cit­ing Noah Smith, is to dereg­u­late America’s own in­dus­try so that more peo­ple make drones there, rather than to im­pose ex­port re­stric­tions. {064-R08}
The same goes for India. If local doc­tors are not good enough, whip them into shape through com­pe­ti­tion rather than ban­ning for­eign doc­tors, “be­cause then the pa­tient will die”.
~ Varma ad­mit­ted he had no so­lu­tion to Chinese IP theft or the threat to Taiwan. “You gotta do some­thing,” he said.

quote.text: The third glob­al­i­sa­tion is no more glob­al­i­sa­tion than crony cap­i­tal­ism is cap­i­tal­ism.

sections.label: What comes next
sections.head: Two months’ head start
sections.caption: where sanctions bite
body: Export con­trols are not new, Ajay Shah said. They were part of how the West won the Cold War. Cut off, the USSR tried self-reliance and never caught up: it could not build com­put­ers or CPUs, and never got to Unix. {064-C10}
Recreating a vast body of knowl­edge is hard, he said, and au­thor­i­tar­ian regimes crush the tiny 0.01 per cent of ge­niuses, “the mav­er­icks”, who might have man­aged it.
Still, a de­ter­mined coun­try can do a lot with weaker equip­ment. Parallel com­put­ing strings to­gether hun­dreds of CPUs, and that ca­pa­bil­ity ex­ists in India, China and Russia. {064-C11}
## Races and tar­gets

Against a fixed tar­get such as a nu­clear bomb, Shah said, sanc­tions are use­less. In a race, they may mat­ter: a lag of a month or two in drone de­sign could let Ukrainian drones beat Russian and Chinese ones on the bat­tle­field. {064-C12}
Amit Varma warned that the logic sounds great but the real world re­acts. Squeezing China could make it more des­per­ate over Taiwan, and China is ramp­ing up legacy chips. {064-C13}
He re­called America fund­ing guer­ril­las in Afghanistan against the Soviet Union, Osama bin Laden among them. “And look what hap­pened.” {#afghan}
~ Shah agreed that sur­prises are com­ing. Most chips in­side a drone are sim­ple legacy chips, he added, so China may end up dom­i­nat­ing them glob­ally.

quote.text: Instead of 10 super duper pow­er­ful mod­ern Nvidia GPUs, you’ll have 1000 weaker GPUs, you will get to the same com­pute.

Part one, it’s very dif­fi­cult to recre­ate a vast body of knowl­edge and ar­ti­facts. Part two, the peo­ple who would have done it are the ones that get hurt the most by an au­thor­i­tar­ian regime.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Chess computers, used cars, banned workstations and a cluster of cheap chips

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how NSE did it with cheap chips
stories.head: Beowulf versus Chicago
body: In the early 1990s, the National Stock Exchange was about to start trad­ing eq­uity de­riv­a­tives. It wanted a risk man­age­ment sys­tem never seen be­fore: one that ran in real time, and cov­ered not just each clear­ing mem­ber but every sin­gle par­tic­i­pant.

Chicago had the two great de­riv­a­tives ex­changes, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and the Chicago Board of Trade. NSE sent Ashish Chauhan, now its CEO, and Susan Thomas to study their risk sys­tems and pick one to buy.

They came home unim­pressed. Thomas told NSE’s lead­er­ship, Ravi Narayan and Chitra Ramakrishna, that the Chicago sys­tems were 1970s tech­nol­ogy, “dull, ob­so­lete stuff”. NSE could do bet­ter with a Beowulf clus­ter: many cheap Intel CPUs com­put­ing in par­al­lel.

It works, Ajay Shah ex­plained, be­cause one participant’s risk does not de­pend on another’s. Amit Varma’s cal­cu­la­tion can run on one CPU and the pro­ducer Nomsita’s on a sec­ond. Varma said nei­ther he nor Nomsita un­der­stood “that par­al­lel what­ever”, but he was happy their power had been mul­ti­plied. {064-J03}

NSE’s IT lead­er­ship thought it crazy, and real time im­pos­si­ble. “People in the room all came to blows,” Shah said. Ravi Narayan split the dif­fer­ence: he would fund Thomas to build a proof of con­cept at IGIDR.
The bar was set at 100 cal­cu­la­tions a sec­ond, be­yond what the in­cum­bents thought pos­si­ble. {#hundred} Built with Shovam Mishra, the sys­tem, called PRISM, suc­ceeded.
~ Endlessly re­worked, PRISM still runs the risk man­age­ment of NSE’s de­riv­a­tives trad­ing today.
stories.why: If a job splits into in­de­pen­dent pieces, many cheap pro­ces­sors can match a few elite ones. That is why Shah thinks block­ing top-end chips mostly makes a de­ter­mined country’s work slower and more painful, not im­pos­si­ble. {064-S04}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on how NSE built PRISM

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a black market he thought was history
stories.head: Nudge nudge, wink wink, Nvidia
body: Before 1991, Ajay Shah re­called, mod­ern elec­tron­ics were ex­otic in India. Protectionism kept them out, and peo­ple re­lied on elab­o­rate in­for­mal chains, some would say a black mar­ket, and on friends trav­el­ling abroad.

His most amaz­ing pur­chase was an early chess com­puter: you moved the pieces, and an LED blinked to show its reply. A neigh­bour fly­ing to Singapore brought it home. “I had the same one,” Amit Varma said.
You would think that was a dis­tant mem­ory, Shah said. Instead, in Shanghai today you go nudge nudge, wink wink, to find the dealer who has the right Nvidia A100. {064-S01}
~ Kazakhstan has a big­ger black mar­ket for a wider array of chips, where peo­ple fly in from New Delhi car­ry­ing a suit­case of chips to sell for a profit. {#kazakh}
stories.why: Trade bar­ri­ers do not make tech­nol­ogy van­ish; they push it un­der­ground. The world thought it had fin­ished with that kind of pro­tec­tion­ism, Shah said, and now ex­port con­trols aimed at China have brought it back.
stories.postscript: Varma, re­call­ing the pre­vi­ous episode on knowl­edge lost and re­gained, called it “the same shit all over again”. {064-R10}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the black market for chips

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on India’s own years under export controls
stories.head: No Sun for India
body: Export con­trols are not a weapon in­vented for China. In the late 1980s, Ajay Shah re­called, the lat­est Sun SPARCstation work­sta­tions were not li­censed for ex­port to India. If you were in India, you could not buy one. {064-S03}
“Now this is a piti­fully weak CPU by mod­ern stan­dards,” he said. “But ex­port con­trols was a thing.”
Until Manmohan Singh and George W. Bush signed the nu­clear deal, the foot­print of ex­port con­trols on Indian buy­ers was ex­ten­sive. Some re­main even now.

~ The Bureau of Industry and Security, Shah said, had been fad­ing into a less con­se­quen­tial agency. It has since been res­ur­rected and am­pli­fied, on a scale he never saw even in the Cold War. {#resurrected}
stories.why: India once lived on the wrong side of ex­port con­trols, and the West’s Cold War block­ade of the USSR set the tem­plate. What is new, in Shah’s telling, is the sheer scale of today’s cam­paign.
stories.postscript: At its Cold War peak the agency is­sued about 100,000 ex­port li­cences a year, Amit Varma said; in the 1990s, 10,000; now, 40,000. {#forty}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on India under export controls

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s one fact about the pre-1991 economy
stories.head: Second-hand, first in line
body: For lis­ten­ers born after 1991, Amit Varma had one fact to show how bizarre the old closed econ­omy was: a sec­ond­hand car cost more than a new one. {064-S02}
The rea­son was the queue. A new car came with a wait­ing list of seven years. A used car was avail­able im­me­di­ately.

“It didn’t mat­ter what the con­di­tion was,” Varma said. The price re­flected the value, “as it were”. He pointed lis­ten­ers to an episode of his pod­cast *The Seen and the Unseen* on the 1991 re­forms, with Ajay Shah and Shruti Rajagopalan.

~ He told the story as a warn­ing. With in­dus­trial pol­icy, tar­iffs and pro­tec­tion­ism back be­tween the US and China, he said, “it al­most feels as if the world is going back­wards”. {#backwards}

quiz.a: That two coun­tries with McDonald’s never go to war; Russia and Ukraine both had them.

quiz.q: What did Susan Thomas propose to NSE instead of buying a Chicago exchange’s risk system?
quiz.a: A Beowulf clus­ter: many cheap Intel CPUs com­put­ing each participant’s risk in par­al­lel.

quiz.q: Against what kind of goal, by Ajay Shah’s account, are export controls useless?
quiz.a: A fixed tar­get like a nu­clear bomb; they can mat­ter only in races.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 64. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Deng Xiaoping (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Xi Jinping (Presidencia de la República del Ecuador, public domain); 1972 Nixon visit to China (ron Schumaker, public domain); Janet Yellen (US Department of the Treasury, public domain); Christopher Miller (Gage Skidmore, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: When the Chips Are Down
shelf.creator: Pranay Kotasthane and Abhiram Manchi
shelf.why: Together with Chip War, it de­mys­ti­fies the semi­con­duc­tor wars and what is re­ally going on be­neath the head­lines.

shelf.title: Chip War
shelf.creator: Chris Miller
shelf.why: It ex­plains the semi­con­duc­tor wars, the core bat­tle­field of the US–China tech con­flict dis­cussed in the episode.

shelf.title: How China Escaped the Poverty Trap
shelf.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
shelf.why: Yuen Yuen Ang’s ac­count of what ac­tu­ally hap­pened in China, which backs Amit’s re­fusal to take a car­i­ca­tured, good-versus-evil view of a deeply com­plex coun­try.

shelf.title: China’s Gilded Age
shelf.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
shelf.why: Amit calls both of Ang’s books crit­i­cal for un­der­stand­ing China’s re­cent decades with­out fall­ing into sim­plis­tic nar­ra­tives.

shelf.title: Michael Pettis interviewed by Forward Guidance
shelf.creator: Forward Guidance (with Michael Pettis)
shelf.why: Pettis lives in China and, in Ajay’s words, gets this stuff deeply.

shelf.title: The U.S. Finally Has a Strategy to Compete With China. Will It Work?
shelf.creator: Greg Ip
shelf.why: Amit calls it a won­der­ful piece that lays out the what and how of the shift, from a bi­par­ti­san pro-trade, en­gage-China con­sen­sus to a new bi­par­ti­san con­sen­sus that America is at war with China.

shelf.title: ‘An Act of War’: Inside America’s Silicon Blockade Against China
shelf.creator: Alex W Palmer
shelf.why: It shows how far the US now reaches: goods made and shipped en­tirely out­side America, with no US com­po­nents, can still count as American goods if American tech­nol­ogy or soft­ware was used to make them.

shelf.title: Three holes in the U.S.’ economic strategy against China
shelf.creator: Noah Smith
shelf.why: It makes the point Amit wants: in­stead of ex­port re­stric­tions, America could dereg­u­late its own in­dus­try so more peo­ple build drones at home.

shelf.title: The tech wars are about to enter a fiery new phase
shelf.creator: The Economist
shelf.why: It ar­gues, cor­rectly in Amit’s view, that these tech and trade wars are bad for the US, bad for China and bad for the rest of the world.

shelf.title: Knowledge Lost and Knowledge Regained (Episode 63)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It ex­plains why being cut off from global trade and knowl­edge crip­ples a coun­try: it is very hard to make a pen­cil, let alone an iPhone, on your own.

shelf.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left un­done (fac­tor mar­kets, agri­cul­ture), and how free­ing parts of the econ­omy set off the dis­cov­ery and trade be­hind India’s growth spurt.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: The Three Globalizations (Episode 17)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s frame­work of three glob­al­i­sa­tions, from the first era with­out cap­i­tal con­trols, when London bond is­sues built Indian rail­ways, to today’s, where ac­cess to the ad­vanced-economy core de­pends on good be­hav­iour in mil­i­tary and for­eign af­fairs.

shelf.title: Dawn of the third globalisation?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s ‘novel insight’ that glob­al­i­sa­tion isn’t dead: it now runs in­side a club of well-behaved coun­tries, en­forced through eco­nomic state­craft, and ex­cludes rogue play­ers.

shelf.title: The China Model is Broken (Episode 16)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Chinese state con­trol and in­dus­trial pol­icy caused deep prob­lems be­hind the cherry-picked EV and solar suc­cesses: Xi’s cen­tral­i­sa­tion and na­tion­al­ism, cap­i­tal con­trols, real-estate over­build­ing, the exit of for­eign­ers and a failed eq­uity mar­ket.

shelf.title: The case for trade barriers against Chinese imports
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The writ­ten case be­hind the hosts’ most un­com­fort­able dis­agree­ment: why a com­mit­ted free trader like Ajay wor­ries about a sys­tem­i­cally im­por­tant, rule-breaking re­vi­sion­ist power.

shelf.title: The BIS list of sanctions
shelf.creator: Bureau of Industry and Security
shelf.why: Anyone in busi­ness should know who is on the list.

shelf.title: The Outlaws (Episode 61)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Stories of mav­er­icks such as Semmelweis, Mendel and Darwin who were ig­nored by the es­tab­lish­ment and vin­di­cated late, some­times at the cost of lives.

shelf.title: The Semiconductor Wars (Episode 358 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Abhiram Manchi
shelf.why: It is a long-form deep dive on chips to ac­com­pany the book rec­om­men­da­tions.

laughs.text: Amit on the ex­port-control agency: ‘At the risk of being sanc­tioned by the US BIS, I will say that the US BIS should be re­named US BS.’

Ajay ex­plains par­al­lel com­put­ing by not­ing that the cal­cu­la­tion for Amit is in­de­pen­dent of the one for pro­ducer Nomsita. Amit: ‘nei­ther me nor Nomsita un­der­stood ex­actly that par­al­lel what­ever you were say­ing. But you spoke about mul­ti­ply­ing our power, so I’m kinda happy with that.’

Ajay on India ne­go­ti­at­ing a free trade agree­ment with Switzerland: ‘the humor of this is the Swiss have no tar­iffs against any­thing from India. So what are you going to ne­go­ti­ate? The Swiss say we are al­ready at zero.’
The old say­ing that two coun­tries with McDonald’s never go to war. Ajay: ‘Well, Russia in­vaded Ukraine and both coun­tries had McDonald’s.’
Ajay’s sketch of the post-1989 eu­pho­ria: ‘This en­tire night­mare of 2000 years of fight­ing be­tween Persia and Athens has come to an end, and Athens won.’
